overview: The K-way Merge pattern is an algorithmic design template used to traverse, merge, or query elements across $K$ pre-sorted datasets (such as arrays, linked lists, or matrix rows). By placing the smallest (head) element of each of the $K$ lists into a Min-Heap, the algorithm can retrieve the global minimum in $O(1)$ time. Popping the minimum element from the heap and immediately inserting the next item from the corresponding list allows the heap to maintain a constant window of active heads. This pattern reduces the complexity of merging $K$ lists of total size $N$ from a naive $O(K \cdot N)$ or $O(N \log N)$ down to a highly optimized $O(N \log K)$ runtime and $O(K)$ space.
recognition_signals: Multiple Sorted Lists: The problem features $K$ pre-sorted arrays, linked lists, or rows of a matrix.
Merged Output: The goal is to traverse, merge, or find specific elements (like the $K\text{th}$ smallest) across all lists.
Logarithmic Comparison Goals: The target runtime is $O(N \log K)$ with an auxiliary space cap of $O(K)$.
In-Place Priority: The problem requires retrieving values sequentially without fully sorting the combined array.
Smallest Ranges: Finding the tightest range containing at least one element from each of the $K$ lists.
Sorted Matrix Queries: Locating the $K\text{th}$ smallest element in a matrix where both rows and columns are sorted.

mental_model.analogy: Imagine $K$ different conveyor belts carrying sorted items down towards a single packaging table.
mental_model.description:
Imagine **$K$ different conveyor belts** carrying sorted items down towards a single packaging table.

At the merging table, you place a **sorting funnel** that holds exactly $K$ items—one from the front of each conveyor belt. You pick the smallest item from the funnel, pack it, and let it go. The moment a belt's item is packed, the conveyor belt advances, sliding its next sorted item into the empty slot in your funnel. You repeat this process, ensuring that the funnel always contains exactly one item from every active conveyor belt, and that you always pack items in sorted order.

brute_force_journey.brute_force_description: The brute force approach is to copy all elements from the $K$ lists into a single array and sort it.
brute_force_journey.inefficiency_observation: Overlapping subsegments perform duplicate evaluations of identical elements.
brute_force_journey.optimization_concept:
```
  Brute Force
  [Combine all elements into a single array and sort them -> O(N log N)]
       ↓
  Observation
  [The individual arrays are already sorted; we only need to compare their heads]
       ↓
  Optimization
  [Maintain a Min-Heap of size K holding the head of each active array]
       ↓
  Final Pattern
  [Extract min, push the next item from the same array -> O(N log K)]
```

animation_steps.description: Push first element of each of the K sorted lists into the Min-Heap.
Pop minimum element 1 from the heap. Append to result. Push next head from the same list.
Pop next minimum 2 from heap. Append to result.

variants.name: **Merge Sorted Lists**
variants.description: Min-Heap of node pointers (Push the popped node's `next` pointer.)

variants.name: **Kth Smallest in M Lists**
variants.description: Min-Heap of elements (Track index and push `list[index + 1]`.)

variants.name: **Kth Smallest in Matrix**
variants.description: Range Binary Search / Heap (Bisect value range or treat matrix rows as $K$ lists.)

variants.name: **Smallest Range**
variants.description: Min-Heap + Max Tracker (Pop min, update range (`max - min`), push next.)

variants.name: **Largest Pairs Sum**
variants.description: Min-Heap / Max-Heap (Iterate first $K$ elements of sorted arrays to form pairs.)

common_mistakes.description: **Losing origin traceability:** Forgetting to record which list a popped element came from. Without tracking the `list_index`, it is impossible to know which conveyor belt to advance.
**Dereferencing null pointers:** Failing to check if `node->next` is null before pushing it back onto the heap when merging linked lists.
**Matrix Binary Search integer overflow:** Calculating the midpoint of matrix boundaries using `(start + end) / 2` instead of the overflow-safe `start + (end - start) / 2`.
**Incorrect Heap Ordering:** Using a Max-Heap instead of a Min-Heap, which returns the maximum values instead of merging in ascending order.

interview_perspective: Highly popular in FAANG/HFT rounds testing optimized traversals.

cheat_sheet: Always bundle the origin metadata with the value in the heap.

Define a custom node structure containing `(value, elementindex, listindex)` to ensure you can trace popped values back to their source list. For sorted matrix bisection, search the value range instead of the index range to achieve optimal $O(N \cdot \log(\text{max} - \text{min}))$ limits.
